frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d6: On June 4, 1943, President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin once more, and the letter stands as Document 6 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Their correspondence that season mixed war news with the search for a meeting place and time. The record gives the date and the two names and nothing more specific. Readers who want the letter's errand must go to the text, printed in the official Foreign Relations record.
frus-1944-quebec-d6:
President Roosevelt answered Prime Minister Churchill on May 27, 1944, two days after Churchill's message. The reply appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

The last week of May 1944 left the two leaders little room for delay. Invasion forces were sealed in their camps, and the final political choices about France and the Mediterranean had to be made by letter. Roosevelt's answer kept the exchange moving at the speed events required. For readers, this message is part of the paper record of the alliance at its most concentrated moment, just before the landings that Tehran and Cairo had promised.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d6: From Moscow on 24 September 1944, Ambassador Harriman sent President Roosevelt another report, filed as document 6. It appears in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. By that autumn the Red Army was driving westward, and Harriman's reporting from the Soviet capital fed directly into American planning for the next meeting of the Big Three.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d6:
An iron curtain is falling: in this famous telegram of May 12, 1945, Churchill tells Truman he is profoundly concerned about Europe. Half the American air force in Europe, he has learned, has already begun moving to the Pacific. Newspapers are full of the American armies' great movements out of Europe. British forces face marked reduction under earlier plans.

The Canadian Army will certainly leave; the French are weak and hard to deal with. Within a very short time, Churchill warns, Western armed power on the Continent will have vanished, save moderate forces to hold Germany down. Meanwhile, what is to happen about Russia? The telegram that follows in the file answers with the phrase history kept.
tob-0038-d6:
File 100-HQ-440423 is the FBI's headquarters dossier on Dick Gregory, the comedian who became a leading civil rights and antiwar activist. Gregory used his fame to fund marches, fasts, and voter drives. The Bureau watched him for years and kept the paperwork.

Reports, clippings, and memos track his speeches, travels, and campaigns, as agents judged his influence and intent. The file shows the reach of domestic surveillance at its height: a performer filed as a security matter. Released under open-records law, it now serves historians of both Gregory and the surveillance state that followed him.
tob-0039-d6:
The seventh roll of the Doctors' Trial microfilm continues the Nuremberg record of 1946 to 1947. Nazi doctors and administrators were on trial for experiments performed on prisoners. The tribunal's stenographers kept every session, and the microfilm keeps their work.

On this roll the case moves through further witnesses and documentary exhibits, with the defense testing the prosecution's proof. Read in sequence, the rolls show how a court builds guilt or innocence out of paper and memory. The proceedings confronted medicine with its own crimes in a public forum, and the verbatim record remains the surest guide to what was actually said and shown.
frus-1945-50-intel-d6:
Donovan wrote to Samuel Rosenman, the president's special counsel, on 4 September 1945. Rosenman was one of Truman's closest advisers and a channel to the president's ear. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A letter to the president's counsel is a lobbying move, and Donovan was lobbying for the life of his agency and his plan. He wrote outside the chain of command because the chain was not giving him what he wanted. Readers see the personal side of institution building here: access, friendship, and timing used as tools. The letter also shows Donovan working every door in the White House as the decision on the OSS drew near.
frus-1861-d6:
Joseph Wright wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 May 1861. The dispatch is document 6 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861, printed with the President's message to Congress.

Dispatches were the working mail of the age, sent by ship and read weeks after they were written. Wright's report entered the stream of news by which Washington judged Europe's mood. Read in order, such letters show a government learning of its own crisis at a slow, sea borne pace. The mails from Europe took ten days or more, so each dispatch was old news on arrival.
frus-1862-d6:
News and judgment from Charles Francis Adams reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 27 December 1861. It was printed as Document 6 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It was written in the close of the war's first year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d6:
Writing on 27 November 1862, Charles Francis Adams sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The dispatch stands as document 6 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Late November brought the legation a full plate: the war's news from home, the British press, and the acts of Southern agents in Europe. Adams sorted it all for Washington in a calm, plain hand. His letters rarely rose to drama, which is part of their worth. This one shows the steady watch that kept the State Department wise to London's mind.
